policy: All collected records are retained. Unresolved details are research gaps, not grounds for exclusion or a declaration that the record is false.

original.title: Ethiopia drought and food crisis
original.description: After years of failed rains, a severe drought gripped southeastern Ethiopia with 8 million facing severe food shortages. Malnutrition-related deaths ran into the low thousands before international relief averted a repeat of the 1984-85 famine.

retained.title: Ethiopia drought and food crisis
retained.description: After years of failed rains, a severe drought gripped southeastern Ethiopia with 8 million facing severe food shortages. Malnutrition-related deaths ran into the low thousands before international relief averted a repeat of the 1984-85 famine.

review.note: FAO supports the regional drought and roughly eight million needing assistance. No reviewed source establishes 1 March as a discrete event or 2,000 as a measured death toll. Do not convert a broad crisis estimate into a daily count.

original.title: Barakova coal mine explosion
original.description: A methane gas explosion at the Barakova coal mine killed 80 miners. Ukraine's worst mining disaster since independence.

retained.title: Barakova coal mine explosion
retained.description: An explosion at the Barakova coal mine in the Krasnodon region on March 11, 2000 killed dozens of miners. RFE/RL subsequently reported 81 deaths, while contemporary Guardian reporting gave 82.

review.note: The original 80 was an early count. RFE/RL on March 16 reports 81, while The Guardian on March 13 reports 82. The sources do not explain that reduction or establish a reconciled final count. The source-attributed 81 is a candidate correction only; the unresolved exact toll prevents publication.

original.title: Poso sectarian riots
original.description: The third and deadliest phase of the Poso riots between Christian and Muslim communities. An estimated 300 people were killed.

retained.title: Poso sectarian riots
retained.description: The third and deadliest phase of the Poso riots between Christian and Muslim communities. An estimated 300 people were killed.

review.note: HRW identifies May-June 2000 as the third phase and explains that aggregate fatality counts are uncertain. Exact 23 May onset and phase-specific 300 deaths were not established by the reviewed evidence.

original.title: Pushkin Square bombing
original.description: A bomb exploded in a crowded underground passageway beneath Pushkin Square during rush hour, killing 13 people. Linked to Chechen separatists.

retained.title: Pushkin Square bombing
retained.description: A bomb exploded in a pedestrian underpass near Moscow's Pushkin Square during the evening rush hour on 8 August 2000. Officials investigated several possible motives; no group claimed responsibility at the time.

review.note: Contemporary reporting supports date, rush-hour underpass attack and explicitly uncertain responsibility. It gives preliminary deaths, not the later 13. Remove definitive Chechen linkage; final toll still needs a reliable later source.

original.title: Typhoon Bilis
original.description: Super Typhoon Bilis, the strongest typhoon on record to strike Taiwan at the time, made landfall with winds over 200 km/h. It killed 71 people across Taiwan and mainland China.

retained.title: Typhoon Bilis
retained.description: Typhoon Bilis made landfall in southern Taiwan on August 22, 2000 before crossing toward mainland China. NOAA reports winds of about 258 km/h and more than 70 deaths across Taiwan and mainland China.

review.note: NOAA supports 22 August landfall, winds over 200 km/h and over 70 deaths in Taiwan and mainland China; CWA supports the date. Remove unqualified all-time Taiwan intensity record, which depends on measurement and comparison. Exact 71 is not established by the reviewed over-70 source; withhold pending exact mortality evidence.

original.title: Mekong Delta floods
original.description: The worst flooding in the Mekong Delta in decades inundated more than 825,000 homes and affected over 5 million people. 482 people died, most of them children.

retained.title: Mekong Delta floods
retained.description: The worst flooding in the Mekong Delta in decades inundated more than 825,000 homes and affected over 5 million people. 482 people died, most of them children.

review.note: ADRC supports major prolonged flooding and 825,000 inundated homes, but not a discrete 10 September event or final 482 toll. Mekong Commission's later table gives a different national total (453). Geographic and reporting-period reconciliation is required.

original.title: Bangladesh floods
original.description: The worst floods in more than 20 years hit southwestern Bangladesh, drowning over 2 million people across border districts. 130-150 people died from drowning, snakebites, and disease.

retained.title: Bangladesh floods
retained.description: Severe flooding affected western and southwestern Bangladesh in September 2000, forcing large numbers of residents from their homes. The IFRC described major inundation in border districts on 22 September. Contemporary casualty and displacement figures were provisional.

review.note: The description incorrectly says two million drowned: sources describe homelessness or affected population. IFRC dates the major western-border inundation to 22 September; 15 September and 150 deaths are not established. Published counts differ by event scope, so no replacement date or toll is asserted.

original.title: Start of the Second Intifada
original.description: The Second Intifada began after Israeli opposition leader Ariel Sharon visited the Temple Mount compound. By end of 2000, roughly 300 people had been killed.

retained.title: Start of the Second Intifada
retained.description: The Second Intifada began after Israeli opposition leader Ariel Sharon visited the Temple Mount compound. By end of 2000, roughly 300 people had been killed.

review.note: Sharon's visit and the late-September onset are supported, but 300 by year-end is not established by the cited December report, which ends 2 December and separates populations. Need a defined inclusive date range and victim scope; the count is not a 28 September toll.

original.title: Afghanistan Drought and Famine Crisis
original.description: Afghanistan's third consecutive year of severe drought brought the country to the brink of famine, with FAO and WFP reporting that about 5.5 million people faced severe food shortages by mid-2001. World Bank and UN officials warned of famine conditions and reported thousands of deaths from starvation and exposure, though the total death toll was never precisely counted.

retained.title: Afghanistan Drought and Famine Crisis
retained.description: Afghanistan's third consecutive year of severe drought brought the country to the brink of famine, with FAO and WFP reporting that about 5.5 million people faced severe food shortages by mid-2001. World Bank and UN officials warned of famine conditions and reported thousands of deaths from starvation and exposure, though the total death toll was never precisely counted.

review.note: FAO/WFP confirms a third drought year and famine risk. The 5.5 million assistance target is documented in September, not a specific 21 June incident. Neither a 5,000 death toll nor the asserted World Bank attribution is established.

original.title: Southern Peru Earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck off the coast of southern Peru, killing roughly 100 people and injuring more than 1,300, with most deaths in the Arequipa region. The quake triggered a tsunami that killed about two dozen people in the Camaná area and damaged or destroyed thousands of buildings, including historic structures in Arequipa.

retained.title: Southern Peru Earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck off the coast of southern Peru, killing roughly 100 people and injuring more than 1,300, with most deaths in the Arequipa region. The quake triggered a tsunami that killed about two dozen people in the Camaná area and damaged or destroyed thousands of buildings, including historic structures in Arequipa.

review.note: USGS confirms 23 June, Mw 8.4, southern Peru and tsunami. EERI's initial assessment gives 77 dead, 68 missing and 2,713 wounded; the record mixes rounded and preliminary figures. Final deaths versus missing and tsunami subtotal require reconciliation before changing 100.

original.title: Colombo Airport Attack
original.description: LTTE suicide commandos attacked Bandaranaike International Airport and the adjoining air force base near Colombo, killing at least 18 people and destroying or damaging 11-13 aircraft, including several SriLankan Airlines jets. The attack caused an estimated $350 million in losses to the national carrier alone.

retained.title: Colombo Airport Attack
retained.description: LTTE suicide commandos attacked Bandaranaike International Airport and the adjoining air force base near Colombo, killing at least 18 people and destroying or damaging 11-13 aircraft, including several SriLankan Airlines jets. The attack caused an estimated $350 million in losses to the national carrier alone.

review.note: Early reporting gave at least 18 including attackers; later accounts give seven servicemen and 14 attackers. The original does not define its scope and aircraft-loss figures vary. The documented 03:50 local start on 24 July is 23 July UTC (Sri Lanka then UTC+6). Proposed date/location only; resolve toll and damage claims before integration.

original.title: Assassination of Ahmad Shah Massoud
original.description: Two al-Qaeda operatives posing as journalists detonated a bomb hidden in a camera while interviewing Ahmad Shah Massoud, the military leader of the Afghan Northern Alliance, killing him and one other person. The assassination came two days before the September 11 attacks and removed the alliance's most effective commander ahead of the US invasion.

retained.title: Assassination of Ahmad Shah Massoud
retained.description: Two al-Qaeda operatives posing as journalists detonated a bomb hidden in a camera while interviewing Ahmad Shah Massoud, the military leader of the Afghan Northern Alliance, killing him and one other person. The assassination came two days before the September 11 attacks and removed the alliance's most effective commander ahead of the US invasion.

review.note: UNAMA supports the 9 September assassination by attackers posing as journalists. The second non-attacker death and camera-versus-battery concealment require stronger direct evidence; 'most effective commander' is an assessment, not an established factual rank.

original.title: Srinagar Legislative Assembly Attack
original.description: Jaish-e-Mohammed militants rammed a car bomb into the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly complex in Srinagar and stormed the building, killing 38 people and wounding about 60 during a gun battle lasting several hours. No legislators were in the building at the time of the attack.

retained.title: Srinagar Legislative Assembly Attack
retained.description: A vehicle bombing and armed attack struck the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly complex in Srinagar on October 1, 2001. India's Home Ministry subsequently attributed the attack to Jaish-e-Mohammed and recorded 38 deaths. Published casualty breakdowns disagree on whether attackers are included.

review.note: Further research establishes October 1 and the attack identity in an MHA gazette notification, which gives 38 deaths. However, SATP's 2001 assessment includes four attackers within 38, while its 2000-2017 table lists 38 victims plus three attackers (41 total); its timeline also contains 36. These are material scope conflicts, not merely unsupported injury/occupancy prose. Remove the original 60-injured and no-legislators claims, but do not certify a victim-only total.

sources.name: South Asia Terrorism Portal: attack table

original.title: Qala-i-Jangi Fortress Uprising
original.description: Taliban and al-Qaeda prisoners revolted at the Qala-i-Jangi fortress near Mazar-i-Sharif, triggering a six-day battle in which up to 400 prisoners, about 73 Northern Alliance fighters, and CIA officer Johnny Spann — the first American killed in combat in the war — died. Only 86 of the more than 400 prisoners survived, including American Taliban fighter John Walker Lindh.

retained.title: Qala-i-Jangi Fortress Uprising
retained.description: Taliban and al-Qaeda prisoners revolted at the Qala-i-Jangi fortress near Mazar-i-Sharif, triggering a six-day battle in which up to 400 prisoners, about 73 Northern Alliance fighters, and CIA officer Johnny Spann — the first American killed in combat in the war — died. Only 86 of the more than 400 prisoners survived, including American Taliban fighter John Walker Lindh.

review.note: 400 was an upper-end prisoner estimate, not a verified total including Northern Alliance and US deaths. Accounts differ on duration and fighter losses; 86 survivors is reported. A single precise aggregate cannot be inferred from these incompatible estimates.

original.title: Mount Nyiragongo eruption
original.location: Goma, Democratic Republic of the Congo
original.description: Mount Nyiragongo erupted on January 17, 2002, sending lava flows through the city of Goma and forcing hundreds of thousands of residents to flee into Rwanda. Estimates of the death toll range from about 45 to 147, with more than 12,000 homes destroyed and roughly 100,000 people displaced.

retained.title: Mount Nyiragongo eruption
retained.location: Goma, Democratic Republic of the Congo
retained.description: Nyiragongo erupted on January 17, 2002, sending lava through Goma and causing mass evacuation. A Smithsonian report records conflicting mortality assessments: 147 deaths reported by the UN and about 70 estimated by a subsequent medical field investigation. Both include deaths in a petrol-station explosion on January 21.

review.note: The original 100 is not established as an enumerated toll. The Smithsonian report explicitly contrasts a UN count of 147, including 60-100 petrol-station deaths, with Peter Baxter's field assessment of about 70 total and about 20 at the petrol station. This is a substantive contradiction within the same source, not resolved by attribution alone. The proposed 147 is only a documented alternative and must not be published as settled.

original.title: 2002 Gujarat riots
original.description: Weeks of communal rioting followed the Godhra train burning, with violence concentrated in Ahmedabad and other Gujarat cities. The official death toll was about 1,000, while independent estimates range up to 2,000, most of them Muslims.

retained.title: 2002 Gujarat riots
retained.description: Weeks of communal rioting followed the Godhra train burning, with violence concentrated in Ahmedabad and other Gujarat cities. The official death toll was about 1,000, while independent estimates range up to 2,000, most of them Muslims.

review.note: HRW supports mass violence and higher estimates, but its retrospective says retaliatory attacks had already begun on 27 February, before the major 28 February escalation. The rounded official count needs a primary final tally and explicit exclusion/inclusion of Godhra victims to prevent overlap.

original.title: Southern Africa food crisis
original.description: A regional drought, compounded by failed harvests and high HIV/AIDS prevalence, created a severe food crisis across Malawi, Zimbabwe, Zambia and neighboring countries, leaving more than 10 million people in need of emergency food aid. The WHO projected up to 300,000 excess deaths from hunger and related disease in the worst-affected countries.

retained.title: Southern Africa food crisis
retained.description: Southern Africa faced a regional food and health emergency in 2002. WHO warned in August that the crisis could cause 300,000 additional deaths over the following six months; that was a projection, not a measured death toll. WFP later reported that relief helped prevent the food crisis from becoming a famine.

review.note: Critical: 300,000 was WHO's prospective warning of possible additional deaths, not observed mortality. Statements were issued in August/October, not 1 June. No defensible positive replacement toll or daily date established. Quarantine/remove from observed-death totals pending resolution; do not retain the projection as actual deaths.

original.title: Central European floods
original.description: Days of record rainfall in August 2002 caused catastrophic flooding along the Elbe, Danube and Vltava rivers, inundating Dresden, Prague and other cities. About 110 people died across central Europe and Russia, with damages exceeding $15 billion.

retained.title: Central European floods
retained.description: Days of record rainfall in August 2002 caused catastrophic flooding along the Elbe, Danube and Vltava rivers, inundating Dresden, Prague and other cities. About 110 people died across central Europe and Russia, with damages exceeding $15 billion.

review.note: This is a multi-country, multi-day disaster. 13 August is a reporting/peak date rather than established onset. Sources differ on whether Russian floods are included; the stated location omits Russia despite including it in the toll. No consistent 110-death geographic/time scope or $15bn basis established.

original.title: Typhoon Rusa
original.description: Typhoon Rusa, the strongest typhoon to strike South Korea in more than four decades, made landfall near Goheung on August 31, 2002. It killed 238 people across South Korea, Japan and North Korea and caused about $4.2 billion in damage.

retained.title: Typhoon Rusa
retained.description: Typhoon Rusa, the strongest typhoon to strike South Korea in more than four decades, made landfall near Goheung on August 31, 2002. It killed 238 people across South Korea, Japan and North Korea and caused about $4.2 billion in damage.

review.note: JTWC confirms 31 August Goheung landfall. Korean retrospective reports 246 dead or missing in South Korea; that is not interchangeable with 238 confirmed deaths across three countries. Need country-specific dead/missing reconciliation and intensity-superlative definition.

original.title: Moscow theater siege (Nord-Ost)
original.description: Chechen militants seized the Dubrovka theater in Moscow on October 23, taking more than 900 hostages. Russian security forces pumped an incapacitating gas into the building on October 26; at least 130 hostages died, most of them from the gas.

retained.title: Moscow theater siege (Nord-Ost)
retained.description: Chechen militants seized the Dubrovka theater in Moscow on October 23, taking more than 900 hostages. Russian security forces pumped an incapacitating gas into the building on October 26; at least 130 hostages died, most of them from the gas.

review.note: Dates, more than 900 hostages and gas-related deaths are supported. ECHR case material and HRW record 129 while later summaries give 130 or higher; final official 130 and the claimed lower-bound wording need reconciliation, not averaging.

original.title: Outbreak of the Darfur conflict
original.description: Rebel groups attacked a government air base in North Darfur, triggering a counterinsurgency campaign by the Sudanese government and allied Janjaweed militias that killed an estimated 3,000 civilians and displaced more than 600,000 people by the end of 2003. The conflict escalated into a sustained campaign of attacks on civilian villages.

retained.title: Outbreak of the Darfur conflict
retained.description: Rebel groups attacked a government air base in North Darfur, triggering a counterinsurgency campaign by the Sudanese government and allied Janjaweed militias that killed an estimated 3,000 civilians and displaced more than 600,000 people by the end of 2003. The conflict escalated into a sustained campaign of attacks on civilian villages.

review.note: HRW supports conflict beginning in February 2003, but the airfield attack belongs to April 25, not the supplied February 26 date. No checked evidence establishes precisely 3,000 civilian deaths or 600,000 displaced by December 2003. Resolve onset convention and annual scope before publication; do not present this as one day's toll.

sources.name: Human Rights and Human Welfare paper

original.title: Riyadh compound bombings
original.description: Al-Qaeda suicide bombers attacked three foreign residential compounds in Riyadh with car bombs, killing 35 people including nine Americans and wounding more than 160. The attacks marked the beginning of a militant campaign inside Saudi Arabia.

retained.title: Riyadh compound bombings
retained.description: Al-Qaeda suicide bombers attacked three foreign residential compounds in Riyadh with car bombs, killing 35 people including nine Americans and wounding more than 160. The attacks marked the beginning of a militant campaign inside Saudi Arabia.

review.note: Rewards for Justice explicitly reports 35 killed, including nine Americans, but another US government chronology reports 34 including nine attackers. Their fatality populations do not clearly align. Date, three compounds and al-Qaeda attribution are supported; victim-only versus attacker-inclusive scope needs resolution before accepting 35.

original.title: Znamenskoye truck bombing
original.description: Suicide bombers drove an explosives-laden truck into the government administration compound in Znamenskoye, northern Chechnya, destroying the local FSB headquarters and killing about 59 people, including children. It was one of the deadliest attacks of the Chechen conflict, later claimed by rebel commander Shamil Basayev.

retained.title: Znamenskoye truck bombing
retained.description: A suicide truck bombing struck a government and security compound in Znamenskoye, Chechnya, on May 12, 2003. A UN chronology records 59 people killed. The attack also injured about 200 people.

review.note: UN chronology supports May 12 and 59 deaths. Checked sources do not establish the claim that Basayev claimed responsibility. Remove that assertion rather than converting allegations into fact; exact attacker inclusion is not specified in the UN total. That unresolved attacker/victim scope remains a publication blocker despite the supported shorter prose.

original.title: Boumerdès earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck offshore near Zemmouri in Boumerdès Province, northern Algeria, killing about 2,266 people and injuring more than 10,000. It was the strongest earthquake to hit Algeria since 1980 and left roughly 200,000 people homeless.

retained.title: Boumerdès earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck offshore near Zemmouri in Boumerdes Province on May 21, 2003, causing extensive destruction in northern Algeria. Algeria's CRAAG reports 2,365 deaths, while other summaries give 2,266; the totals are not reconciled here.

review.note: Full CRAAG text confirms May 21 at 19:44 local time and Mw 6.8, but reports 2,365 deaths, not the original/reference-summary figure of 2,266. The earlier ledger note missed this contradiction. No source-level reconciliation establishes a final total. Remove the ranking, injury and homelessness precision, and withhold the row pending mortality reconciliation.

original.title: Yangtze and Huaihe river floods
original.description: Seasonal floods along the Huaihe and Yangtze river basins in central and eastern China inundated large areas of Anhui, Jiangsu, and Henan provinces during the summer, killing about 1,551 people and affecting more than 100 million. It was the worst flooding in China since the 1998 Yangtze floods.

retained.title: Yangtze and Huaihe river floods
retained.description: Seasonal floods along the Huaihe and Yangtze river basins in central and eastern China inundated large areas of Anhui, Jiangsu, and Henan provinces during the summer, killing about 1,551 people and affecting more than 100 million. It was the worst flooding in China since the 1998 Yangtze floods.

review.note: 1,551 is the nationwide annual flood total across 30 provincial-level areas, not an established Huaihe/Yangtze event toll. MFA reported 676 nationwide by July 20. July 1 onset and the Anhui-only location are unsupported for this aggregate. Must choose an event-specific scope and date before replacing the count.

original.title: Second siege of Monrovia
original.description: LURD rebels besieged the Liberian capital Monrovia from June to August 2003, shelling civilian neighborhoods, churches, and schools and killing an estimated 1,000 to 1,500 civilians. The siege ended when President Charles Taylor went into exile and international peacekeepers arrived.
sources: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

retained.title: Second siege of Monrovia
retained.description: LURD rebels besieged the Liberian capital Monrovia from June to August 2003, shelling civilian neighborhoods, churches, and schools and killing an estimated 1,000 to 1,500 civilians. The siege ended when President Charles Taylor went into exile and international peacekeepers arrived.
sources: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

review.note: Sources describe several June-July offensives and a July 18-August siege, not a clearly named second siege with a 1,500 final civilian toll. HRW documents hundreds killed and over 2,000 injured, while the summary gives 1,000 killed. Dates, episode naming and civilian estimate need reconciliation.

original.title: European heat wave
original.description: An extreme heat wave across Western and Central Europe, peaking in the first half of August, caused an estimated 70,000 excess deaths, including about 15,000 in France. Temperatures exceeded 40 degrees Celsius for consecutive days, and most victims were elderly people living without air conditioning.
sources: French Institute for Public Health Surveillance (InVS)

retained.title: European heat wave
retained.description: Extreme heat affected Europe during summer 2003, with a major peak in August. A retrospective study estimated more than 70,000 excess deaths over the summer, including deaths before August; this is a seasonal excess-mortality estimate rather than a single-day toll.
sources: French Institute for Public Health Surveillance (InVS)

review.note: Peer-reviewed estimate concerns excess mortality over summer 2003; more than 20,000 excess deaths preceded August. August 1 cannot anchor the whole mortality interval without an explicit convention. The air-conditioning/majority claim is unsupported and removed; toll is an estimate, not certified heat deaths.

sources.name: Robine et al., UKHSA research portal
Robine et al., full paper via WMO

original.title: Mumbai twin bomb blasts
original.description: Twin car bombs exploded at the Gateway of India and the Zaveri Bazaar jewellery market during the lunch hour, killing 52 people and injuring more than 200. Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba was suspected, and three people were later convicted for the attack.

retained.title: Mumbai twin bomb blasts
retained.description: Twin car bombs exploded at the Gateway of India and the Zaveri Bazaar jewellery market during the lunch hour, killing 52 people and injuring more than 200. Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba was suspected, and three people were later convicted for the attack.

review.note: Later court reporting disagrees: 54 in New Indian Express versus 52 in AFP/Dawn; even the reference summary conflicts internally. Date, targets and three convictions are corroborated, but the final incident-only toll needs a court or police source distinguishing other blasts in the prosecution.

original.title: Imam Ali Mosque bombing in Najaf
original.description: A car bomb exploded outside the Imam Ali Mosque in Najaf as worshippers left Friday prayers, killing Ayatollah Mohammed Baqir al-Hakim and about 95 people and wounding more than 200. It was one of the deadliest attacks in Iraq since the fall of Baghdad.

retained.title: Imam Ali Mosque bombing in Najaf
retained.description: A bombing outside the Imam Ali shrine in Najaf on August 29, 2003, killed Ayatollah Mohammed Baqir al-Hakim and many other worshippers. Iraq Body Count records a range of 83-126 deaths; contemporary reporting gave differing totals.

review.note: 95 includes al-Hakim, not 95 plus him. PBS updated contemporary count to 95 with 142 wounded; IBC retains 83-126 deaths. Exact final count and over-200 injury claim remain unsettled. Proposed prose preserves the range instead of pretending a final total is established.

original.title: Istanbul bombings
original.description: Al-Qaeda truck bombers attacked two synagogues in Istanbul on November 15 and the British Consulate and HSBC headquarters on November 20, killing 57 people and wounding more than 700. They were the deadliest terrorist attacks in Turkish history.

retained.title: Istanbul bombings
retained.description: Truck bombings targeted two Istanbul synagogues on November 15, 2003, and the British consulate and HSBC offices on November 20. The attacks were linked to al-Qaeda. Reported death totals vary, including whether the four bombers are counted.

review.note: Two attack dates are established, but later totals differ: BBC summary 58; detailed reference 59 including four bombers; original 57 not reconciled. Remove the unqualified all-time Turkish superlative. Count covers both November 15 and 20, not only the indexed date.

original.title: Bam earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 6.6 earthquake destroyed the ancient city of Bam in southeastern Iran, killing about 26,271 people and injuring roughly 30,000. More than 85% of the city's buildings collapsed, and the quake was Iran's deadliest disaster in decades.

retained.title: Bam earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 6.6 earthquake struck Bam and surrounding communities in southeastern Iran on December 26, 2003. It destroyed much of the city and killed tens of thousands. Published fatality totals differ; the World Bank's reconstruction report used approximately 26,000.

review.note: Magnitude 6.6 and December 26 UTC are supported. Fatality accounts conflict: World Bank about 26,000, Iranica 31,824-43,000, and the reference summary cites later 34,000 versus an earlier revised 26,271. Do not silently treat one precise figure as settled. The 1990 Iranian quake also makes 'deadliest in decades' unsafe.

original.title: Al Hoceima earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 6.5 earthquake struck near the Mediterranean port city of Al Hoceima in northern Morocco, destroying about 2,500 homes and leaving more than 15,000 people homeless. The final death toll was 628, with 926 people injured.

retained.title: Al Hoceima earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 6.4 earthquake struck near Al Hoceima in northern Morocco on February 24, 2004. A subsequent regional support committee report recorded 628 deaths and 926 injuries. Thousands of homes were destroyed and more than 15,000 people displaced.

review.note: USGS gives Mw 6.4, not 6.5. ADRC preserves the March official count of 628 and 926 injured; another reference gives 631, so attribute 628 to that report rather than call it an uncontested final toll. UTC earthquake date is February 24. The later 631 figure is not reconciled with the March snapshot; changing the prose's attribution alone does not establish final mortality. Withhold pending that reconciliation.

original.title: Ashura bombings in Karbala and Baghdad
original.description: Coordinated suicide bombings, car bombs and small-arms attacks struck Shia worshippers commemorating Ashura at shrines in Karbala and Baghdad, killing at least 182 people and wounding more than 550. It was one of the deadliest attacks in Iraq since the fall of Saddam Hussein.

retained.title: Ashura bombings in Karbala and Baghdad
retained.description: Coordinated explosions struck Shia worshippers observing Ashura in Karbala and Baghdad on March 2, 2004. Contemporary reports gave differing casualty totals, including 182 deaths; hundreds were injured.

review.note: Contemporary RTE reports 182, while Japan's retrospective diplomatic bluebook says over 170 with over 390 injured; final 182/550 is not established. Initial weapon accounts were disputed. Correct geographic scope and remove speculative tactical detail.

original.title: Darfur genocide (2004 killings)
original.description: The armed conflict in Darfur, in which the Sudanese government and allied Janjaweed militias systematically attacked civilian villages, killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than a million during 2004. United Nations and WHO estimates of deaths in 2004 ranged from about 30,000 to 71,000, mostly from violence, starvation and disease.

retained.title: Darfur genocide (2004 killings)
retained.description: The armed conflict in Darfur, in which the Sudanese government and allied Janjaweed militias systematically attacked civilian villages, killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than a million during 2004. United Nations and WHO estimates of deaths in 2004 ranged from about 30,000 to 71,000, mostly from violence, starvation and disease.

review.note: 70,000 was WHO's estimated mortality among displaced people from living conditions in accessible Darfur areas during March-mid-October 2004, excluding violent deaths. It is neither all 2004 killings nor a July 30 event. Need a defensible interval, title and mortality scope; avoid overlap with the 2003 onset record.

original.title: Typhoon Rananim
original.description: Typhoon Rananim, the strongest typhoon to hit the Chinese mainland since 1956, made landfall in Zhejiang Province, collapsing thousands of homes and triggering floods and landslides. At least 164 people were killed and 24 reported missing in Zhejiang, with nearly 13 million people affected.

retained.title: Typhoon Rananim
retained.description: Typhoon Rananim made landfall in Zhejiang on August 12, 2004, causing destructive winds, floods and landslides. Xinhua's August 16 tally reported 164 deaths and 24 missing in Zhejiang; later summaries give a higher death count.

review.note: 164 dead and 24 missing was the August 16 snapshot, also used by HKO, while later summaries give 168 in China. The 1956 comparison applies to Zhejiang, not all mainland China. Date of landfall is established, but final toll needs reconciliation.

original.title: Rizhskaya metro station bombing
original.description: A female suicide bomber detonated an explosive device near the Rizhskaya metro station in Moscow, killing 10 people and wounding more than 50. The attack, linked to Chechen separatist militants, came one week after the bombing of two Russian passenger planes.

retained.title: Rizhskaya metro station bombing
retained.description: A female suicide bomber detonated an explosive device near the Rizhskaya metro station in Moscow, killing 10 people and wounding more than 50. The attack, linked to Chechen separatist militants, came one week after the bombing of two Russian passenger planes.

review.note: Contemporary reports give ten total deaths; later accounts differ on whether that includes the bomber and accomplice. Russian reference explicitly includes both, while AP wording suggests a larger victim-only count. Date and location established; do not silently equate totals with innocent victims.

original.title: Hurricane Jeanne flooding in Haiti
original.description: Torrential rains from Tropical Storm Jeanne triggered catastrophic flash flooding and mudslides in Haiti, most severely in the coastal city of Gonaives, which was left largely submerged. The Haitian government's final tally recorded 3,006 deaths, including 2,826 in Gonaives, with about 200,000 people affected.

retained.title: Hurricane Jeanne flooding in Haiti
retained.description: Torrential rains from Tropical Storm Jeanne triggered catastrophic flash flooding and mudslides in Haiti, most severely in the coastal city of Gonaives, which was left largely submerged. The Haitian government's final tally recorded 3,006 deaths, including 2,826 in Gonaives, with about 200,000 people affected.

review.note: NOAA confirms catastrophic Haiti flooding and over 3,000 deaths, but exact 3,006/2,826 and the asserted final-government provenance were not established from accessible primary text. NHC report fetch was blocked; archive search found it but not its casualty discussion. September 18 is an onset label for flooding extending into September 19.

original.title: Second Battle of Fallujah
original.description: US, British and Iraqi forces launched Operation Phantom Fury to recapture the insurgent-held city, in the bloodiest battle of the Iraq War up to that point. More than 1,000 people were killed overall, including roughly 1,200-1,500 insurgents, 107 coalition troops, and an estimated 581-670 civilians per Iraq Body Count (about 800 per the Red Cross), and most of the city was destroyed.
sources: International Committee of the Red Cross

retained.title: Second Battle of Fallujah
retained.description: US-led forces launched an offensive against insurgents in Fallujah in November 2004. Civilian and combatant death estimates vary, and available civilian counts cover different areas and periods. Iraq Body Count records 581-670 civilian deaths in nine neighborhoods.
sources: International Committee of the Red Cross

review.note: Numeric 1,000 is not a defensible overall count when the prose itself gives larger combatant losses before civilians. IBC's 581-670 covers nine neighborhoods, not a complete battle census; the reported 800 was an anonymous unofficial Red Cross estimate, not a verified ICRC institutional total. Need consistent full-battle population and interval.

original.title: Philippines typhoon series and Quezon floods
original.description: A series of four typhoons and tropical storms, including Tropical Depression Winnie and Typhoon Nanmadol, brought torrential rain to the Philippines in late November and early December, triggering massive floods and landslides in Quezon Province. The storms killed 1,060 people and left 566 missing, according to the World Health Organization, with most deaths caused by Winnie.

retained.title: Philippines typhoon series and Quezon floods
retained.description: Several tropical cyclones caused severe flooding and landslides in the Philippines in November and early December 2004. A December WHO report recorded 1,060 deaths and 559 missing. Winnie caused much of the destruction, including in Quezon Province.

review.note: WHO release reproduced by ScienceDaily gives 1,060 dead and 559 missing, not 566, as a December snapshot. NASA establishes several storms over November-December and Winnie on November 29. November 30 is not a substantiated onset for the series, and Quezon alone does not describe its total scope.

original.title: Zarand earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 6.4 earthquake struck near Zarand in Kerman Province, Iran, levelling several mud-brick mountain villages and killing 612 people. An estimated 80,000 people were affected and more than 900 were injured.

retained.title: Zarand earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 6.4 earthquake struck near Zarand in Kerman Province, Iran, levelling several mud-brick mountain villages and killing 612 people. An estimated 80,000 people were affected and more than 900 were injured.

review.note: USGS supports Mw 6.4 and February 22. Summary attributes 612 deaths to PAGER-CAT but also reports an independent ISNA count of 799. Need source-level resolution of mortality scope and the 80,000 affected/900 injured figures before full verification.

original.title: Hilla suicide car bombing
original.description: A suicide car bomb exploded beside a queue of police recruits waiting outside a health clinic in Hilla, Iraq, killing 125 people and wounding about 130, many of them civilians shopping in a nearby market. It was the deadliest single attack in Iraq since the 2003 invasion at the time.

retained.title: Hilla suicide car bombing
retained.description: A suicide car bombing struck people waiting outside a clinic in Hilla on February 28, 2005, including applicants for government security jobs. Early reports counted at least 125 dead; Iraq Body Count's current incident table records 135-136.

review.note: 125 was early reporting. IBC's current table gives 135-136 although its heading still says 125-136; another summary gives 127. Date and clinic bombing are secure, final fatality total is not. Remove superlative and broad victim characterization.

original.title: Nias-Simeulue earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 8.6 earthquake struck off the west coast of Sumatra, Indonesia, causing heavy destruction on Nias Island and killing an estimated 1,300 people, with hundreds killed on Simeulue and the Banyak islands. A small tsunami and widespread building collapses added to the casualties.

retained.title: Nias-Simeulue earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 8.6 earthquake struck off northern Sumatra on March 28, 2005, severely damaging Nias and nearby islands and generating a relatively small tsunami. Published death estimates vary; most fatalities occurred on Nias.

review.note: Magnitude 8.6 and March 28 UTC are secure. Later summaries span 915-1,314 while early relief estimates were higher; hundreds on Simeulue/Banyak are not established as final confirmed counts. Need final regional breakdown rather than combining initial estimates.

original.title: Niger food crisis
original.description: Severe drought and a locust infestation triggered a food crisis in Niger affecting 3.6 million people, with UNICEF reporting 32,000 severely malnourished children under five facing death without treatment. A final death toll was never established; UN officials said thousands of children had already died, with overall mortality estimates ranging from several thousand to tens of thousands.

retained.title: Niger food crisis
retained.description: Severe drought and a locust infestation triggered a food crisis in Niger affecting 3.6 million people, with UNICEF reporting 32,000 severely malnourished children under five facing death without treatment. A final death toll was never established; UN officials said thousands of children had already died, with overall mortality estimates ranging from several thousand to tens of thousands.

review.note: No checked source establishes 10,000 crisis-attributable deaths or a July 1 onset. UNICEF and the national mortality survey describe malnutrition, treatment and rates; children at risk are not observed fatalities. Do not infer a toll by multiplying treatment mortality or projected deaths. Numeric entry requires exclusion from aggregates pending evidence.

original.title: Sharm el-Sheikh bombings
original.description: Three bombs exploded in the Red Sea resort town of Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, including two car bombs that hit the Old Market and a hotel in Naama Bay, killing 88 people and wounding about 200. Most of the dead were Egyptians, and it was Egypt's deadliest terrorist attack at the time.

retained.title: Sharm el-Sheikh bombings
retained.description: Bombs struck Sharm el-Sheikh shortly after 01:00 on July 23, 2005, local time, July 22 UTC. Targets included the Old Market and a hotel. Death reports differed: the official count was 64, while hospitals reported 88.

review.note: 01:15 Egyptian summer time July 23 equals 22:15 UTC July 22. IFRC's later report uses 64 deaths and 124 injured, while hospital-based accounts reported 88 and 200. Correct UTC date but retain fatality conflict explicitly.

original.title: Mumbai floods
original.description: A record 944 mm of rain fell on Mumbai in 24 hours, flooding the city and much of Maharashtra state, halting rail, road and air transport and killing approximately 1,094 people. The flood was among the heaviest in the region's recorded history.

retained.title: Mumbai floods
retained.description: Exceptional rain on July 26-27, 2005, caused severe flooding in Mumbai and other parts of Maharashtra. The Santacruz observatory measured 944 mm over 24 hours. Reported mortality totals differ in geographic and flood-related disease coverage.

review.note: 944 mm is the Santacruz station's 24-hour measurement, not citywide rainfall. 1,094 is commonly a Maharashtra-wide count, while some papers incorrectly or differently label it Mumbai-only; NIDM distinguishes municipal deaths. Establish regional/flood-versus-disease scope before accepting exact toll.

original.title: Al-Aaimmah bridge stampede
original.description: A stampede on the Al-Aaimmah bridge in Baghdad during a Shia pilgrimage killed at least 965 people, mostly women and children crushed or drowned in the Tigris River after rumours of a suicide bomber sparked panic. The stampede followed mortar fire near the Kadhimiya shrine that had already killed pilgrims.

retained.title: Al-Aaimmah bridge stampede
retained.description: A stampede on the Al-Aaimmah bridge in Baghdad during a Shia pilgrimage killed at least 965 people, mostly women and children crushed or drowned in the Tigris River after rumours of a suicide bomber sparked panic. The stampede followed mortar fire near the Kadhimiya shrine that had already killed pilgrims.

review.note: 965 appears in retrospective summaries, while contemporary RTE gives 956 and forecasts 1,000. Need final official count and confirmation that earlier mortar victims are excluded. This was a crowd crush triggered by a reported bomber rumor, not an established suicide bombing; terrorism categorization needs taxonomy review.

original.title: Hurricane Stan
original.description: Hurricane Stan triggered torrential rain and catastrophic mudslides across Guatemala, El Salvador and southern Mexico, burying entire villages including Panabaj near Lake Atitlan, where about 1,400 residents were declared missing and presumed dead. More than 1,600 people were killed across the region, most of them in Guatemala.

retained.title: Hurricane Stan
retained.description: Hurricane Stan triggered torrential rain and catastrophic mudslides across Guatemala, El Salvador and southern Mexico, burying entire villages including Panabaj near Lake Atitlan, where about 1,400 residents were declared missing and presumed dead. More than 1,600 people were killed across the region, most of them in Guatemala.

review.note: NOAA authors distinguish 80 direct Stan deaths from 1,000-2,000 deaths in the broader regional weather system. October 5 is near dissipation, not landfall; the Panabaj estimate and exact 1,660 aggregate are not established. Needs explicit regional episode scope and onset.

original.title: Kashmir earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck near Muzaffarabad in Pakistani-administered Kashmir, collapsing tens of thousands of poorly built homes and schools and killing an estimated 75,000 people in Pakistan and more than 1,300 in India, with regional estimates reaching 87,000. About 3.5 million people were left homeless.

retained.title: Kashmir earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck near Muzaffarabad in Pakistani-administered Kashmir, collapsing tens of thousands of poorly built homes and schools and killing an estimated 75,000 people in Pakistan and more than 1,300 in India, with regional estimates reaching 87,000. About 3.5 million people were left homeless.

review.note: Original 75,000 does not match its own Pakistan-plus-India narrative. OCHA uses over 73,000 in Pakistan; other sources give 87,350 and higher regional totals. Magnitude/date established; final geographic and mortality-estimate basis must be chosen explicitly.

original.title: Delhi serial bombings
original.description: Three bombs exploded within half an hour at Paharganj market, on a DTC bus in Govindpuri and at Sarojini Nagar market in New Delhi, killing at least 67 people and injuring more than 200. The blasts occurred days before the Diwali festival.

retained.title: Delhi serial bombings
retained.description: Three bombs struck the Paharganj and Sarojini Nagar markets and a bus in the Govindpuri/Kalkaji area of Delhi on October 29, 2005, shortly before Diwali. Later reporting differs on the final death and injury totals.

review.note: PTI court coverage supports 67 deaths/over 225 injured, but other court reporting gives 62 and over 100; TOI gives 67/105. Original half-hour timing also conflicts with 17:30 to18:05 reporting. Core toll conflict is unresolved; remove unsupported tight timing.

original.title: Darfur conflict (ongoing genocide and humanitarian crisis)
original.description: Armed conflict between government-aligned Janjaweed militias and rebel groups continued across Darfur throughout 2006, marked by attacks on civilians, mass displacement and a severe humanitarian crisis. A September 2006 study published in the journal Science estimated at least 200,000 deaths since the conflict began in 2003, with estimates up to 300,000-400,000 cited by the UN Secretary-General and other organizations, most deaths resulting from violence, disease and starvation. The Darfur Peace Agreement signed in May 2006 failed to end the fighting, and more than two million people remained displaced.

retained.title: Darfur conflict (ongoing genocide and humanitarian crisis)
retained.description: Armed conflict between government-aligned Janjaweed militias and rebel groups continued across Darfur throughout 2006, marked by attacks on civilians, mass displacement and a severe humanitarian crisis. A September 2006 study published in the journal Science estimated at least 200,000 deaths since the conflict began in 2003, with estimates up to 300,000-400,000 cited by the UN Secretary-General and other organizations, most deaths resulting from violence, disease and starvation. The Darfur Peace Agreement signed in May 2006 failed to end the fighting, and more than two million people remained displaced.

review.note: Science publication date is September 15, 2006, not an event onset. Its mortality estimate is cumulative since 2003 and would overlap earlier Darfur records; January 1,2006 is unsupported as a specific event date. Primary study and GAO discuss uncertainty; do not treat 200,000 as additional deaths during 2006.

sources.name: Hagan and Palloni, Death in Darfur

original.title: Al-Askari shrine bombing triggers sectarian violence
original.description: Bombers dressed as security personnel detonated explosives inside the al-Askari shrine in Samarra on February 22, 2006, destroying the golden dome of one of Shia Islam's holiest sites. The blast itself killed no one, but it triggered waves of retaliatory sectarian killings across Iraq, with more than 1,000 people dead within days and hundreds of mosques attacked; leaked U.S. military documents later indicated the death toll exceeded 3,000, and the bombing is widely regarded as having ignited Iraq's civil war.

retained.title: Al-Askari shrine bombing triggers sectarian violence
retained.description: Bombers dressed as security personnel detonated explosives inside the al-Askari shrine in Samarra on February 22, 2006, destroying the golden dome of one of Shia Islam's holiest sites. The blast itself killed no one, but it triggered waves of retaliatory sectarian killings across Iraq, with more than 1,000 people dead within days and hundreds of mosques attacked; leaked U.S. military documents later indicated the death toll exceeded 3,000, and the bombing is widely regarded as having ignited Iraq's civil war.

review.note: Shrine blast itself killed nobody. Subsequent1000/1300/3000 estimates refer to different periods/areas and cannot become a single Samarra bombing toll; they also overlap annual Iraq record. Need a bounded reprisal-event definition. Do not fabricate a positive bombing death count to satisfy schema.

original.title: Iraq sectarian civil war (deadliest year of the conflict)
original.description: Sectarian violence between Shia and Sunni communities escalated sharply after the February 22 bombing of the al-Askari shrine, plunging Iraq into civil war conditions characterized by car bombings, executions, death squads and forced displacement. The Iraq Body Count project recorded about 29,000 violent civilian deaths in 2006, making it the deadliest year of the war since 2003, with the United Nations reporting similar monthly tolls; more than 400,000 people were displaced within Iraq during the year.
sources: United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq (UNAMI)

retained.title: Iraq sectarian civil war (deadliest year of the conflict)
retained.description: Sectarian violence intensified in Iraq in 2006. Iraq Body Count's current database records 29,526 civilian deaths from violence during the full calendar year. This annual total includes numerous separately recorded attacks and is not the toll of the February 22 shrine bombing.
sources: United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq (UNAMI)

review.note: IBC current annual table gives29,526 for all2006; February22 indexes a catalyst, not the start of that count. January-February deaths and other discrete events overlap. UNAMI uses a different methodology, not simply matching IBC. Annual/single-event schema and double counting must be resolved.

original.title: Borujerd (Silakhor) earthquake
original.description: An earthquake of magnitude 6.1 struck the Silakhor plain region of Lorestan province in western Iran on March 31, 2006, early in the morning, centered near the village of Darb-e Astaneh. The quake killed about 70 people, injured more than 1,200 and damaged or destroyed buildings in roughly 330 villages, with the worst destruction in Borujerd and Dorud.
sources: International Institute of Earthquake Engineering and Seismology (IIEES)

retained.title: Borujerd (Silakhor) earthquake
retained.description: An earthquake of magnitude 6.1 struck the Silakhor plain region of Lorestan province in western Iran on March 31, 2006, early in the morning, centered near the village of Darb-e Astaneh. The quake killed about 70 people, injured more than 1,200 and damaged or destroyed buildings in roughly 330 villages, with the worst destruction in Borujerd and Dorud.
sources: International Institute of Earthquake Engineering and Seismology (IIEES)

review.note: Early IFRC and JICA reports give70; IFRC's April2007 retrospective instead gives63 deaths and1,418 injured. Mainshock March31 01:17UTC and Mw6.1 established, but revised mortality discrepancy is not reconciled.

original.title: Mumbai train bombings
original.description: Seven bombs hidden in pressure cookers exploded on crowded Western Line suburban commuter trains in Mumbai during evening rush hour on July 11, 2006. The coordinated attacks killed 209 people and injured more than 700, making them among the deadliest terrorist attacks in India's history; the Indian government blamed the Pakistan-based group Lashkar-e-Taiba.

retained.title: Mumbai train bombings
retained.description: Seven explosions struck suburban trains on Mumbai's Western Line during the evening rush hour on July 11, 2006. Later court reporting gives 189 deaths, differing from the 209 figure in some earlier accounts. Responsibility and the prosecution evidence have been disputed in court.

review.note: Modern court coverage gives189 deaths/824 injured rather than209. The High Court rejected the prosecution case in July2025; subsequent Supreme Court stay did not itself establish guilt. Remove asserted pressure-cooker mechanism and categorical attribution; final victim count requires reconciliation.

original.title: North Korea floods and food crisis
original.description: Torrential rains and three major storms in mid-July 2006 caused severe flooding and landslides across North Korea, particularly in South Pyongan, North Hwanghae and Kangwon provinces, destroying about 31,000 houses and inundating tens of thousands of hectares of farmland. Official reports indicated about 600 people dead or missing, while a UN assessment recorded far lower figures and unverified claims reached thousands; the loss of an estimated 100,000 tonnes of food raised fears of famine, and the government rejected most international relief offers.
sources: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)

retained.title: North Korea floods and food crisis
retained.description: Floods struck several North Korean provinces in July 2006, damaging homes, farmland and infrastructure. Published death and missing-person counts differed widely, and independent assessment was limited.
sources: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)

review.note: 600 conflates uncertain killed/missing reporting. Sources range from Red Cross151 dead to a pro-North Korean newspaper's549 dead/295 missing; outside claims are unverified. WFP describes assistance stocks used for2006 floods, so blanket rejection of relief is misleading. Exact episode onset and toll remain unresolved.

original.title: Ethiopia floods (Dire Dawa and Omo Valley)
original.description: Unusually intense seasonal rains in August 2006 caused two major flood disasters in Ethiopia: a flash flood of the Dechatu River in the city of Dire Dawa on August 6 killed 256 people with about 250 missing, and flooding of the Omo River in the remote South Omo Valley on August 13 killed 364 people and submerged five villages. Combined flood deaths across the country in 2006 reached about 640, with roughly 118,000 people affected and tens of thousands displaced.
sources: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)

retained.title: Ethiopia floods (Dire Dawa and Omo Valley)
retained.description: Unusually intense seasonal rains in August 2006 caused two major flood disasters in Ethiopia: a flash flood of the Dechatu River in the city of Dire Dawa on August 6 killed 256 people with about 250 missing, and flooding of the Omo River in the remote South Omo Valley on August 13 killed 364 people and submerged five villages. Combined flood deaths across the country in 2006 reached about 640, with roughly 118,000 people affected and tens of thousands displaced.
sources: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)

review.note: IFRC's August response reported639, not640; AfDB's full2006 account includes later floods and about900 deaths. Do not merge August and annual scopes. August6 is the local Dire Dawa date, not established onset of all nationwide flooding or confirmed UTC date.

original.title: Abidjan toxic waste dumping (Probo Koala)
original.description: Around August 19, 2006, the tanker Probo Koala, chartered by the Dutch commodities firm Trafigura, discharged about 500 tonnes of chemical waste containing sulphur compounds and petroleum slops at roughly 17 open-air sites around Abidjan, Ivory Coast. The dumping caused at least 17 deaths and led an estimated 100,000 people to seek hospital treatment for nausea, respiratory difficulties, skin lesions and other symptoms; the resulting scandal caused the Ivorian government to resign, and a UN investigation found prima facie evidence linking the waste to the deaths and illnesses.

retained.title: Abidjan toxic waste dumping (Probo Koala)
retained.description: Waste discharged from the Probo Koala was dumped by a local contractor at multiple sites around Abidjan on August 19, 2006. UNEP records more than 100,000 medical consultations afterward. Reported death counts and the extent of medically established causal links differ between sources.

review.note: UNEP describes528 cubic metres and12 sites, Amnesty at least18 sites and an official15-death report, while17 appears in later government-attributed summaries. More than100,000 consultations are not proof of100,000 poisoning hospitalizations. Exact mortality and causal attribution remain unsettled; preserve distinctions.

original.title: Iraq War (2007)
original.description: 2007 was the second-deadliest year of the Iraq War. Iraq Body Count documented 26,112 violent civilian deaths during the year, driven by sectarian violence, vehicle bombings, and the U.S. troop surge launched in February 2007. Approximately 900 U.S. service members were also killed, making 2007 the deadliest year for coalition forces.

retained.title: Iraq War (2007)
retained.description: Iraq Body Count's current database records 26,112 civilian deaths from violence during calendar year 2007. This full-year total includes separately recorded attacks and is not a death count for January 1.

review.note: 26,112 matches current IBC annual database, not January1 deaths. January1 is an annual-index placeholder and cannot be verified as a discrete event date. Remove unsupported causal assertion linking annual deaths to surge and military-death comparison; annual total overlaps individual attacks.

sources.name: Iraq Body Count current annual database

original.title: al-Shorja market bombing
original.description: A suicide truck bomber detonated a vehicle packed with explosives in the al-Shorja market district of central Baghdad on February 3, 2007, killing at least 135 people and injuring more than 300. The blast destroyed shops and vehicles in one of the city's largest markets on a weekend shopping day.

retained.title: al-Sadriya market bombing
retained.description: A suicide truck bomb struck Baghdad's Sadriya market on February 3, 2007. Contemporary reports and an FBI retrospective give at least 135 deaths, while Iraq Body Count's current incident record gives 136-137.

review.note: Wrong market: Sadriya, not Shorja. FBI retrospective records135; current IBC136-137. Date and afternoon timing secure, but exact mortality not reconciled. Correct identity without treating conflicting final counts as settled.

original.title: Battle of Mogadishu (2007)
original.description: In March-April 2007, Ethiopian and Somali government forces launched a major offensive against Islamist insurgents in Mogadishu, prompting heavy urban fighting that killed approximately 1,200 civilians in the capital. The year as a whole was the deadliest of the insurgency, with estimates of more than 6,000 people killed in Mogadishu in 2007.

retained.title: Battle of Mogadishu (2007)
retained.description: Ethiopian and Somali government forces fought insurgents in Mogadishu during major offensives in March and April 2007. Human Rights Watch documented extensive civilian harm but said precise mortality figures could not be established.

review.note: HRW dates main first offensive March29-April2, second round endingApril26, and explicitly cannot give precise civilian deaths. Estimates400-1,000 first round plus about300 second are not an independently established1,200. March21 onset and annual6,000/superlative remain unverified.

original.title: Cyclone Yemyin and Pakistan floods
original.description: Cyclone Yemyin made landfall on Pakistan's Makran coast on June 26, 2007, bringing torrential rain and flash floods that killed about 730 people in Balochistan, Sindh, and the North-West Frontier Province, with more than 100 killed in Afghanistan. Preceding heavy rain had already caused flooding and hundreds of deaths in Karachi.

retained.title: Cyclone Yemyin and Pakistan floods
retained.description: Cyclone Yemyin made landfall on Pakistan's Makran coast on June 26, 2007, bringing torrential rain and flash floods that killed about 730 people in Balochistan, Sindh, and the North-West Frontier Province, with more than 100 killed in Afghanistan. Preceding heavy rain had already caused flooding and hundreds of deaths in Karachi.

review.note: 730 is a Pakistan-wide multistorm/flood figure in secondary summaries, not established as deaths from June26 Yemyin alone. IFRC documents storms fromJune23 and later flooding; final-report body retrieval failed. Need exact geographic/date scope and independently supported mortality before publication.

original.title: Qahtaniya Yazidi community bombings
original.description: Four suicide truck bombers attacked the Yazidi towns of Qahtaniya and Jazira in Nineveh Province, Iraq, on August 14, 2007, killing 796 people and wounding more than 1,500. The coordinated blasts, which destroyed entire residential blocks, remain the deadliest car bomb attack of the Iraq War.

retained.title: Qahtaniya Yazidi community bombings
retained.description: Coordinated suicide vehicle bombings struck Yazidi communities near Sinjar, including Qahtaniya and Jazira, on August 14, 2007. Hundreds of people died. Published mortality figures differ substantially, and the exact total remains unresolved in this audit.

review.note: IBC currently records516-525, versus796 in secondary summaries attributed to Red Crescent and lower government/early counts. Primary Red Crescent documentation establishing796 was not located. Event date/towns and coordinated attacks supported; final count and1,500 injuries unresolved.

original.title: Peru earthquake
original.description: A magnitude 8.0 earthquake struck off Peru's central coast on August 15, 2007, killing 595 people and injuring more than 2,000. The city of Pisco was hardest hit, with about 85 percent of its buildings destroyed, and the quake also caused tsunami flooding along the coast.

retained.title: Peru earthquake
retained.description: A magnitude 8.0 earthquake struck off central Peru on August 15, 2007, severely damaging Pisco and nearby communities and producing a tsunami. A USGS-funded research report cites an October 2007 Peruvian statistical count of 595 deaths, with missing people listed separately.

review.note: USGS-supported research report cites595 deaths plus318 missing as an October2 INEI figure; these are separate categories. Other summaries repeat519, so attribute595 explicitly rather than universal final count. Replace85percent destroyed with supported general damage; date23:40UTC unchanged. The differing 519/595 accounts have not been reconciled by reporting period and finalization; the attributed candidate prose does not by itself establish final mortality. Withhold pending that reconciliation.

original.title: Greek forest fires
original.description: Widespread forest fires in Greece, most severely in the Peloponnese, burned from late August 2007 and killed 85 people across the country. Flames raced through villages, and many victims were trapped in their homes or while fleeing by car.

retained.title: Greek forest fires
retained.description: Widespread forest fires in Greece, most severely in the Peloponnese, burned from late August 2007 and killed 85 people across the country. Flames raced through villages, and many victims were trapped in their homes or while fleeing by car.

review.note: 85 is a summer/season total in secondary accounts, not established for fires beginningAugust24. European Commission study gives76 for2007, while secondary accounts distinguish67 inAugust. Need authoritative mortality reconciliation and defined episode start; July fires cannot be silently moved toAugust24.

original.title: Baghlan bombing
original.description: A suicide bomber attacked a ceremony at a sugar factory in Baghlan Province, Afghanistan, on November 6, 2007, killing about 79 people, including six members of parliament and a number of children. A crowd of politicians and local officials had gathered for the event.

retained.title: Baghlan bombing
retained.description: A bombing targeted a parliamentary delegation visiting a sugar factory in Baghlan on November 6, 2007. Many children and several lawmakers died. UN reporting found that police and bodyguard gunfire after the explosion added to the casualties; the exact number killed by each cause was not established.

review.note: UNAMA's contemporaneous record and later Secretary-General report distinguish bombing deaths from subsequent police/bodyguard gunfire and use roughly70, not79. Exact split and final total remain uncertain; do not assign all deaths to bomber. UN investigation statements also differed before later reporting.

original.title: Cyclone Sidr
original.description: Cyclone Sidr struck Bangladesh on November 15, 2007, with sustained winds of about 215 km/h and a storm surge exceeding five meters in places. The official death toll was 3,447, with some estimates as high as 15,000; the districts of Barguna and Patuakhali were hardest hit.

retained.title: Cyclone Sidr
retained.description: Cyclone Sidr struck Bangladesh on November 15, 2007, causing destructive winds and coastal flooding. Officially reported death counts changed between assessments. Early fears that the toll might reach 15,000 were estimates, not confirmed fatalities.

review.note: 3,447 is a November20 provisional official count, later repeated by GFDRR; ADRC records3,363 onDecember29 and World Bank later3,406.15,000 was a feared early estimate, not a confirmed alternative tally. Date secure; final reported deaths/missing reconciliation remains needed.

original.title: Algiers bombings
original.description: Two car bombs exploded about ten minutes apart in Algiers on December 11, 2007, one near the Supreme Constitutional Court and one beside UN offices, killing 41 people, including 17 UN staff members, and injuring about 170. Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb claimed responsibility.

retained.title: Algiers bombings
retained.description: Two car bombs struck Algiers on December 11, 2007, near the Constitutional Court and UN offices. The United Nations confirms that 17 of its staff were killed. Published overall death counts differ.

review.note: UN confirms17 staff andDecember11; anniversary message says20minutes between bombs, not10.37 is later official total, while secondary41 and early hospital67 differ. Exact overall toll cannot be established from UN staff-only memorial; remove unsupported exact interval.

original.title: Kenya post-election violence
original.description: After the disputed 27 December 2007 presidential election, in which Mwai Kibaki was declared winner over Raila Odinga, weeks of ethnic and political violence engulfed Kenya in January-February 2008, concentrated in Nairobi, the Rift Valley, Western, and Nyanza provinces. Attacks involved machetes, arson, and police gunfire, killing an estimated 1,100-1,500 people (official inquiries later counted about 1,133-1,220 deaths), displacing some 300,000-600,000 people, and triggering a UN-brokered power-sharing agreement in February 2008.

retained.title: Kenya post-election violence
retained.description: Violence followed Kenya's disputed December 2007 election and continued into February 2008. The Waki commission recorded 1,133 deaths during its December 27, 2007-February 29, 2008 assessment period. The toll includes killings across multiple provinces, not one January 1 incident.

review.note: Waki commission supports1,133 deaths in the December27-February29 inquiry period. January1 is not the onset; reported first violence, declaration and inquiry dates differ. Correct toll/geographic scope, but do not replace uncertain onset with another unqualified date. Mediation was African Union-led, not simply UN-brokered.

original.title: Kandahar dog-fighting show suicide bombing
original.description: A suicide bomber detonated explosives in a crowd of several hundred people watching a dog-fighting competition near Kandahar on 17 February 2008, in an attack believed aimed at a local anti-Taliban auxiliary police commander, Abdul Hakim Jan, who was killed with his guards. The blast killed more than 100 people and wounded about 100 others, making it the deadliest single bombing in Afghanistan since 2001; Kandahar's governor confirmed the toll exceeded 100 as wounded victims died. No group claimed responsibility, though the Taliban denied involvement.

retained.title: Kandahar dog-fighting show suicide bombing
retained.description: A suicide bombing struck a crowd watching a dog-fighting competition near Kandahar on February 17, 2008. A local police commander was among those killed. UNAMA recorded 67 civilian deaths, while provincial reporting gave a higher overall toll.

review.note: UNAMA annual report records67 civilian deaths; governor's contemporary account reports over100 overall. Armed police/guards may explain some difference but no reconciled breakdown was obtained.100 is not an exact count when source says over100. Date and gathering supported; attribution/ranking can be omitted but mortality remains core blocker.

original.title: Typhoon Fengshen (Frank) and MV Princess of the Stars sinking
original.description: Typhoon Fengshen swept across the central Philippines from 20-23 June 2008 with winds up to 175 km/h, causing flooding, landslides, and sea surges. Its deadliest impact came when the passenger ferry MV Princess of the Stars, which had sailed from Manila into the storm, capsized off Sibuyan Island on 21 June, killing roughly 800-850 of the estimated 850-920 people aboard. Including the ferry and flood victims, the Philippine government and UN recorded at least 1,371 deaths in the Philippines and China, with hundreds missing, making it the deadliest Philippine typhoon since 2006.

retained.title: Typhoon Fengshen (Frank) and MV Princess of the Stars sinking
retained.description: Typhoon Fengshen crossed the Philippines beginning on June 20, 2008, causing destructive flooding. During the storm, the ferry MV Princess of the Stars capsized near Sibuyan Island on June 21. Philippine disaster-agency reporting in July counted 557 deaths apart from the ferry disaster; a reconciled final combined toll is not established here.

review.note: The June 20 Philippine landfall is supported by HKO; June 25 was the later China landfall. NDCC reporting gives 557 deaths excluding the ferry (GMA, July 10), whereas ADRC's July 31 snapshot also lists 87 missing. The original 1,371, the ferry's asserted 800-850 deaths, and the Philippines/China aggregation were not reconciled with a final official passenger and casualty accounting. Do not add bodies recovered, presumed deaths and missing passengers indiscriminately. The shortened description removes the unsupported attribution of 1,371 to government/UN and the superlative; the numeric toll remains unresolved.

sources.name: Hong Kong Observatory: tropical cyclones in 2008
GMA News: NDCC damage and casualty report, July 10, 2008
Asian Disaster Reduction Center: Philippines typhoon record

original.title: Indian embassy bombing in Kabul
original.description: A suicide car bomber rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the gates of the Indian embassy in Kabul on the morning of 7 July 2008, killing 58 people and wounding about 140, most of them Afghan civilians queuing for visas. Among the dead were four Indian embassy staff, including the defence attaché and press counsellor, six Afghan police officers, and reportedly eight schoolchildren. The attack, blamed on elements of the Afghan Taliban and Pakistan-based militant networks, was one of the deadliest in Kabul during the war.

retained.title: Indian embassy bombing in Kabul
retained.description: A suicide vehicle bombing struck the Indian embassy in Kabul on the morning of July 7, 2008. India's foreign ministry identified four Indian officials and one Afghan embassy employee among those killed. UNAMA subsequently recorded 55 civilian deaths; reported overall totals differ.

review.note: July 7 morning and the embassy identity are supported by MEA. Four Indian officials and one Afghan employee were killed, so four Indian staff is not the entire embassy-staff toll. MEA's 2008-09 annual report says about 60 Afghan nationals plus five embassy personnel; UNAMA's annual report counts 55 civilians, while secondary accounts give 58 overall. These differing populations and totals cannot be assumed equivalent. A previously indexed 2010 MEA PDF returned a 404 on opening and is not treated as primary verification of 58. Removed unsupported police/child subtotals, queue composition and superlative; overall toll remains unresolved.

sources.name: Ministry of External Affairs: annual report 2008-2009
Ministry of External Affairs: foreign relations 2008, July 7 statement
UNAMA: protection of civilians annual report 2008
Wikipedia: 2008 Indian embassy bombing, secondary comparison

original.title: Azizabad airstrike
original.description: US-led coalition forces called in air strikes, including from an AC-130 gunship, on the village of Azizabad in Shindand district, Herat Province, on 22 August 2008, during an operation against a suspected Taliban commander. The Afghan government and the UN (UNAMA) said about 90 civilians were killed, including 60 children and 15 women, based on witness accounts and video evidence; the US military initially denied civilian deaths before a second inquiry acknowledged 33 civilians killed. The incident, which President Hamid Karzai condemned, became a flashpoint over civilian casualties and led Afghanistan to pay compensation to victims' families.

retained.title: Azizabad airstrike
retained.description: A US-led operation struck Azizabad in Herat Province at approximately 02:00 local time on August 22, 2008 (August 21 UTC). UNAMA's annual report subsequently counted 92 civilian deaths, including 62 children. The civilian death toll remained disputed between investigations.

review.note: AIHRC places the attack at approximately 02:00 Afghanistan time on August 22, corresponding to August 21 UTC; propose the UTC correction without changing the original identity key. UNAMA's later annual report gives 92 civilian deaths including 62 children, not the initial 90/60, while the US investigation reported 33. The competing investigations have not been reconciled and 90 cannot be certified as a final total. Remove unverified compensation and aircraft detail, retain the contradiction in notes, and withhold the row pending a settled toll policy/evidence.

sources.name: Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission: report submitted to UN Human Rights Council
UNAMA: protection of civilians annual report 2008
Wikipedia: Azizabad airstrike, competing investigation totals

original.title: Chinese melamine milk scandal
original.description: In September 2008 it emerged that infant formula produced by Sanlu Group and other dairies had been adulterated with melamine, an industrial chemical added to watered-down milk to boost apparent protein content, causing kidney stones and acute kidney failure in infants. China's Ministry of Health confirmed at least 6 infant deaths and reported that nearly 300,000 infants had been sickened, over 50,000 hospitalized at the peak. The government withdrew 8,300 tons of tainted products and arrested dozens of executives and officials.

retained.title: Chinese melamine milk scandal
retained.description: In 2008, melamine deliberately added to diluted milk contaminated infant formula and other milk products in China. A WHO-authored review reported six deaths, 294,000 affected children and 51,900 cumulative hospitalizations as of December 1, 2008. The exact beginning of the contamination and resulting illness was unknown; the problem became public in September.

review.note: The WHO-authored review supports six reported deaths, 294,000 cases and 51,900 cumulative hospitalizations as of December 1, not 50,000 people simultaneously hospitalized at the peak. It says the illness/contamination onset is unknown, with complaints in December 2007 and a first death in May 2008. September 17 marks Singapore's first detection outside China, not the start of the Chinese scandal. No replacement exact onset date is established.
